content.overview: Hospitalization for at least 48 h may be useful for patients with acute myocarditis and heart failure (HF), especially with elevated troponins or initial cardiac dysfunction/arrhythmias. Treat HFrEF if systolic LV dysfunction is present; continue standard HF therapy for at least 6 months after stabilization. Immunosuppression is indicated only in selected cases of acute myocarditis.

table_34_summary.recommendation: Start HF therapy when LV systolic dysfunction is present at presentation.
table_34_summary.duration: Continue for at least 6 months upon complete functional recovery (EF >50%).
table_34_summary.notes: Applies to HFrEF in the presence of systolic LV dysfunction.

table_34_summary.recommendation: Immunosuppression for acute myocarditis with clinical or EMB evidence of autoimmune disease.
Do not use immunosuppression routinely in acute myocarditis without clinical or EMB evidence of autoimmune disease.
table_34_summary.exceptions: Initial empirical IV corticosteroids may be considered when high suspicion of immune-mediated myocarditis, especially if complicated by acute HF, malignant arrhythmias, or high-degree AV block.

table_34_summary.recommendation: Avoid intense sporting activities while symptoms, elevated cardiac enzymes, or ECG/imaging abnormalities are present.
table_34_summary.duration: Avoid for at least 6 months after complete recovery.
Yearly follow-up for at least 4 years with ECG and echocardiography.
table_34_summary.rationale: Acute myocarditis may lead to dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) in up to 20% of cases.

key_terms_and_abbreviations_used_on_page.HFrEF: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
